agent_response.summary: Candidate 7 builds on validated candidate 6 (scope "assemble", k=1). The per-frequency assembly loop now also produces the explicit conjugate transpose A^H of each signal matrix. The batched solve section takes it ready-made instead of building a 0.9 GB transposed copy at top level. Candidate 6 (1d5a796f) passed official and strict. Physical outputs were exact and the gradient's maximum absolute error was 4.547e-13, the same as the parent's. First run was 23.558 s versus the parent's 24.657 s (−1.10 s, one run, not repeat-confirmed). Forward execution fell to 9.31 s from 11.51 s, gradient execution rose to 2.12 s from 1.81 s, compile rose 0.78 s, warm median was 12.39 s (13.80) and RSS 10.8 GB (12.5). This is the first non-default value of the operator to pass strict. Nothing was run locally.
agent_response.hypothesis: The forward saving in candidate 6 came from doing full-size elementwise and strided copies per frequency, where the data stays in cache. The A^H transpose-conjugate is one more such copy of about 0.9 GB. Building it inside the loop should cut forward execution a little more, by roughly 0.1–0.4 s (unmeasured), with compile and reverse time about the same. Transpose and conjugate are exact. The risk is that A's gradient now adds its contributions from the loop path and the batched solves in a different order, which could shift the gradient at rounding level and fail strict. That would show that only assembly can go inside the loop.
agent_response.notes: The notes file has candidate 6's full results and the corrected explanation: the assembly loop speeds up the forward pass, and the large reverse-pass savings of candidates 1–3 came from the solves in the loop, which is the part that fails strict. Candidate 6 is the best validated revision of this session and needs repeat runs before any claim that it is reliably faster. If candidate 7 fails strict or is slower, I'll revert to candidate 6's code and finish the operator spec and handoff. About 31 minutes remain.
